title: Optional stopping
objectives: Use the optional stopping theorem to find ruin probabilities and expected durations without first-step equations.

screens.title: Stop at either end
screens.prose: You have £3 and make fair £1 bets until you reach £10 or go broke. Here are 300 such games; 30 are drawn. The lower panel averages your final bankroll over the first $k$ games. Move the ends with the sliders.

derive.caption: {{values.hitsUp}} of {{values.paths}} games reached the top. Average final bankroll: £{{fixed(values.stopped, 2)}}.

screens.question: With the ends at £0 and £10, what share of games reach £10? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Read the count in the top left of the chart.
Divide the games that hit the top by 300.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the number that reached the top by 300.

byKey.even: A fair bet does not make the two ends equally likely. £0 is 3 bets away, £10 is 7.
byKey.ruin: That is the share that went broke. Read the count for the top.
byKey.ratio: You compared the distances, 3 to 7. The chance is your share of the whole range, 3 out of 10.

explain.text: 97 of 300 games reached £10, a share of 0.32, close to $\tfrac{3}{10}$. The average final bankroll settled at £3.23, near the dashed start line at £3. Fair bets kept their mean even though each game stopped.

screens.title: The mean survives the stop
screens.prose: Each bet is fair, so the bankroll $S_n$ is a martingale. The rule stop at £0 or £10 never looks ahead. The chart says such stopping keeps the mean: $E[S_T] = S_0 = 3$, where $T$ is the step at which you stop.
screens.question: $S_T$ is 10 with chance $P$ and 0 otherwise. What is $P$?

byKey.even: If both ends were equally likely, the mean at the stop would be £5, not £3.
byKey.ruin: $\tfrac{7}{10}$ is the chance of going broke.

explain.text: $E[S_T] = 10P$ and the mean is still 3, so $P = \tfrac{3}{10}$. This is the answer of Gambler's ruin, found with no equations. The whole argument is that stopping cannot change a fair game's mean.

screens.title: Stopping times
screens.prose: A **stopping time** $T$ is a rule that decides at each step $n$ from the first $n$ steps only. The **optional stopping theorem**: for a martingale $M$, $E[M_T] = E[M_0]$ in three cases. (1) $T$ is bounded. (2) $E[T]$ is finite and the steps of $M$ are bounded. (3) The stopped process stays bounded, and $T$ is finite with chance 1.
screens.question: Which rule is a stopping time?

options.text: Stop the first time the bankroll is £0 or £10
Stop one bet before the bankroll first hits £0
options.why: To stop one bet early you must know the next result. The rule looks into the future.

options.text: Stop at the last visit to £5 before the game ends
options.why: You only know a visit was the last once the game has ended.

options.text: Stop at the step where the bankroll will be highest
options.why: The highest point is known only at the end of the game.

hints.text: For each rule, ask whether you can decide at step $n$ using only the bets so far.
A rule that needs a later result is not a stopping time.
Only the first hit of an end is decided by what has happened.

feedback.correct: The first hit of an end. You know it has happened the moment it happens.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A stopping time uses only the past and the present.

byKey.before: This rule needs tomorrow's result today.
byKey.last: This rule needs the rest of the game.
byKey.peak: This rule needs the rest of the game.

explain.text: Whether you have hit £0 or £10 is known from the bets so far, so it is a stopping time. The other rules need results that have not happened. Here condition (3) holds: the stopped bankroll stays between £0 and £10, and the game ends with chance 1.

screens.title: The ruin chance in four lines
screens.prose: Now take a general start $i$, with ends at 0 and $N$. Let $P$ be the chance of reaching $N$ first.
screens.question: Put the argument in order, and leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Every bet is fair, so $S_n$ is a martingale.
$T$, the first hit of 0 or $N$, is a stopping time, the stopped walk stays in $[0, N]$, and $T$ is finite with chance 1. So the theorem applies.
$S_T$ is $N$ with chance $P$ and 0 otherwise, so $E[S_T] = NP$.
The walk is fair, so it is equally likely to end at either end: $P = \tfrac12$.
lines.why: Fair bets do not make the ends equally likely. The nearer end is likelier, and the mean fixes how much.

hints.text: First name the martingale, then check the theorem applies.
Apply the theorem, then write $E[S_T]$ in terms of $P$.
Martingale, stopping time and bound, theorem, two outcomes, solve. Leave out the equal-ends line.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the conditions before you use the theorem.

byKey.x: That line gives $\tfrac12$ from any start, which the chart contradicts.
byKey.left-out: A line that belongs is in the Left out list. Only the equal-ends line should be there.

explain.text: The theorem needs a martingale and a stopping time that meets a condition, so those come first. Then the mean at the stop is $i$, and it is also $NP$. Solving gives $P = \tfrac{i}{N}$.

screens.title: How long it lasts
screens.prose: Now stop $S_n^2 - n$, the martingale from Hidden martingales, at the same $T$. Its steps are bounded inside $[0, 10]$ and $E[T]$ is finite, so condition (2) holds: $$E[S_T^2] - E[T] = 3^2 = 9.$$
screens.question: Use $E[S_T^2] = 10^2 \times \tfrac{3}{10}$. How many bets does the game last on average?

feedback.correct: 21 bets: $i(N - i) = 3 \times 7$. The same formula gives 2,500 bets from £50 of £100.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $E[S_T^2]$, then solve $E[S_T^2] - E[T] = 9$.

byKey.sq: 9 is the start value of the martingale, not the duration.
byKey.dist: 7 bets would be enough only if every bet won.

explain.text: $E[S_T^2] = 30$, so $E[T] = 30 - 9 = 21 = i(N - i)$, as in Gambler's ruin: 25 bets from £5 of £10. These games lasted 20.2 bets on average, and the panel's average is 12.1, within sampling error of 9. From £2 with ends £0 and £5 the formula gives 6.

screens.title: An unfair game
screens.prose: Now each bet wins with chance $p = 0.4$, from £5 with ends £0 and £10. $S_n$ is no longer fair, so stop $r^{S_n}$ with $r = \tfrac{q}{p} = 1.5$. That gives $$r^5 = P\,r^{10} + (1 - P)\,r^0.$$
screens.question: What is $P$, the chance of reaching £10? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $r^5 = P r^{10} + (1 - P)$ with $r = 1.5$.

byKey.plain: $\tfrac{5}{10}$ comes from stopping the plain walk, which is not fair here.
byKey.p: 0.4 is the chance of one win. Reaching £10 needs five more wins than losses.
byKey.flip: You used $r = \tfrac{p}{q}$. That gives the chance of going broke, $1 - P$.

explain.text: $P = \dfrac{1 - 1.5^5}{1 - 1.5^{10}} = \tfrac{32}{275} \approx 0.1164$. On the chart the average of $S_T$ drifts down to about £1.17, while the average of $r^{S_T}$ stays near its start, $r^5 \approx 7.59$. Choose the martingale before you stop.

screens.title: How long an unfair game lasts
screens.prose: For the duration, stop the drift martingale $S_n - (p - q)n$. That gives $E[S_T] - (p - q)E[T] = i$, so $$E[T] = \frac{NP - i}{p - q}.$$ Take $p = 0.6$ from 2 with ends 0 and 4, where $P = \tfrac{9}{13}$.
screens.question: What is $E[T]$? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $NP - i$, then divide by $p - q = 0.2$.

byKey.fair: 4 is $i(N - i)$, the fair answer. With an edge the game ends sooner.
byKey.nodiv: $\tfrac{10}{13}$ is $NP - i$. Divide it by $p - q = 0.2$.

explain.text: $\tfrac{36}{13} - 2 = \tfrac{10}{13}$ and $\tfrac{10}{13} \div 0.2 = \tfrac{50}{13} \approx 3.846$; these games averaged 3.87 steps. At $p = 0.49$ from £50 of £100 the same formula gives about 1,904.1 bets. That is fewer than the fair 2,500, because the drift ends games sooner.

screens.title: Wald's identity
screens.prose: Optional stopping also handles sums. Take independent steps with mean $\mu$, and a stopping time $T$ with finite mean. Then **Wald's identity** says $E[S_T] = \mu\,E[T]$. It comes from stopping the martingale $S_n - n\mu$. The bars show the number of rolls until a die shows 6.
screens.question: You roll a fair die until the first 6. What is the expected total of all the rolls, the 6 included?

hints.text: The number of rolls is geometric with chance $\tfrac16$.
$E[T] = 6$ rolls, and each roll has mean $\mu = 3.5$.

feedback.correct: 21: $3.5 \times 6$. Check: five non-6 rolls averaging 3, then a 6, also gives $15 + 6 = 21$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the mean roll by the expected number of rolls.

byKey.one: 3.5 is one roll. The game lasts 6 rolls on average.
byKey.rolls: 6 is the expected number of rolls, not their total.
byKey.six: You used 6 for every roll. Only the last roll is sure to be a 6.

explain.text: $E[T] = 6$ and $\mu = 3.5$, so Wald gives $E[S_T] = 21$. A second route: the 5 rolls before the 6 average 3 each, giving $15 + 6 = 21$. A seeded run of 200,000 games averaged 21.03.

That is one bet. The game lasts nearly 2,000 bets, and the edge acts on each.
That is the ruin chance, or the answer with $r = \tfrac{p}{q}$.

screens.title: Stops and targets
screens.prose: A trader runs a fair strategy in steps of £1,000. She sets a stop at a loss of £4,000 and a target at a gain of £2,000. In units of £1,000 she starts 4 above the stop and 2 below the target.
screens.question: Fill in her chance of hitting the target, the expected number of trades, and her expected P&L.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shift so the stop sits at 0, then use the fair formulas.

byKey.r2c1: A stop and a target on a fair strategy cannot create an edge.

explain.text: She hits the target with chance $\tfrac23$ after 8 trades on average. Her expected P&L is $\tfrac23 \times 2000 - \tfrac13 \times 4000 = 0$. Stops and targets change the shape of the P&L, not its mean.

ideas: A stopping time decides from the past alone. A stopped martingale keeps its mean if $T$ is bounded, or has finite mean with bounded steps, or stays bounded with $T$ finite.
Stopping $S_n$, $S_n^2 - n$, $(q/p)^{S_n}$ and $S_n - (p - q)n$ gives every ruin chance and duration in one line each.
Wald's identity, $E[S_T] = \mu E[T]$, is optional stopping for sums of independent steps.

formula.name: Optional stopping
formula.note: Fair ruin: $P = \tfrac{i}{N}$, $E[T] = i(N - i)$. Unfair: $P = \tfrac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N}$, $E[T] = \tfrac{NP - i}{p - q}$.

summary.trap: Choose the martingale first: for an unfair walk $S_n$ is not one, and stopping it gives $\tfrac{i}{N}$, which is wrong.

quiz.prose: A trader proposes to close a position at the highest point of its first 10 days.
quiz.question: Is this a stopping time?

options.text: No: on any day she cannot know whether a higher day is still to come
Yes: 10 days is a bounded time
options.why: The rule is bounded, but it needs the future. A stopping time decides from the past alone.

options.text: Yes, if the price is a martingale
options.why: Whether a rule is a stopping time has nothing to do with the process being fair.

feedback.correct: No. The peak is known only after day 10.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Can the rule be applied using only the days so far?

byKey.yes: Bounded is not enough. The decision on day $n$ must use days 1 to $n$ only.

explain.text: To stop at the peak she must know the later days are lower. That needs the future, so it is not a stopping time. A rule like that would beat a fair game, which the theorem forbids.

quiz.prose: You start at £10, already on the upper end, with ends £0 and £10.
quiz.question: What does the duration formula $i(N - i)$ give?

widget.accept: 0: the game is over before it starts

feedback.correct: 0. $T = 0$, and the chance of the top is $\tfrac{10}{10} = 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $i = N = 10$ into $i(N - i)$.

byKey.hundred: You used $N^2$. The factor $N - i$ is 0.

explain.text: $10 \times 0 = 0$, and indeed $T = 0$. The chance formula gives $\tfrac{10}{10} = 1$. Optional stopping agrees: $E[S_T] = S_0 = 10$.

quiz.prose: Fair £1 bets from £4, stopping at £0 or £12.
quiz.question: What is the expected number of bets?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $E[T] = i(N - i)$.

byKey.forty8: You used $i \times N$. The second factor is $N - i = 8$.
byKey.eight: 8 is the distance to the target.

explain.text: Stopping $S_n^2 - n$ gives $E[T] = E[S_T^2] - 16 = 144 \times \tfrac13 - 16 = 32$. That is $i(N - i) = 4 \times 8$.

quiz.prose: Each trade's P&L is independent with mean £30. You stop after the first losing trade, which happens with chance 0.2 on each trade.
quiz.question: What is your expected total P&L?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $E[T]$, then use $E[S_T] = \mu E[T]$.

byKey.one: £30 is one trade. You expect 5 trades.
byKey.four: You counted 4 trades. The losing trade counts too: $E[T] = 5$.

explain.text: The number of trades is geometric with $E[T] = \tfrac{1}{0.2} = 5$. Stopping at the first loss is a stopping time, so Wald gives $30 \times 5 = 150$.
